finding: The live range of $1,500-$4,800 is too low at both ends for a remanufactured automatic transmission on the vehicles checked. Built totals (transmission price without the refundable core charge + stated hours x $120-$160/hr, the national middle labor rate used for these checks): economy 2020 Nissan Versa CVT about $4,175-$5,685 (7.5-12 hr); midsize 2021 Honda Accord CVT about $3,816-$6,012 (6.2-12 hr); truck 2021 Silverado 1500 8-speed about $4,847-$5,671 (5.4-7.4 hr); luxury 2016 Acura MDX 9-speed about $4,653-$7,310 (6.3-10.9 hr). So every total we can build starts above $3,800 and every class tops out above $5,600; the live ceiling of $4,800 is below the bottom of the truck class and below the top of all four. The $1,500 floor is not supported by anything loaded: the cheapest remanufactured unit seen is $3,072 (Honda's own Accord CVT kit at an online discount) before any labor, and the smallest stated labor time is 5.4 hours (about $650 at $120/hr). Benchmarks agree: ConsumerAffairs reports $6,238-$6,764 on average and a shop owner's $3,000-$4,000 even for old four-speed units; Kelley Blue Book says $2,900-$7,100 for a new transmission and $8,143-$8,689 at a dealer for the MDX. A figure near $1,500 looks like a used (salvage-yard) transmission or a rebuild of a simple older unit, not a remanufactured one. A range of roughly $3,800-$7,500 fits what was found; older four- and five-speed vehicles may come in lower, but only one such price was loaded (a remanufactured 2003 Accord 5-speed at $3,499 before labor). Weak points in the parts figures: for the midsize and luxury classes no independent remanufacturer's price could be loaded (no listing for an Accord CVT or an MDX 9-speed was found, and one seller's Accord page would not load), so the low in those two classes is the discounted online price of the maker's own remanufactured unit ($3,072.15 Honda, $3,897.08 Acura) and the high is the same unit at list; both ends therefore come from one dealer-parts retailer per class, and a shop that buys the unit from its local dealer may pay and charge closer to list. A comparable midsize CVT from an independent remanufacturer (2015-2018 Nissan Altima 3.5L) is $4,549, shown for scale only. The midsize prices are for Honda's kit for the 2023 Accord CVT, because the pages for the 2021 kit failed to load; the economy low is a listing for the Nissan Kicks, which Nissan's catalog shows uses the same transaxle as the 2020 Versa; the economy high is a unit Nissan's catalog labels new, though it carries an $800 core charge; the truck's two prices are for different engines (5.3L and 2.7L) with the same 8-speed. Nothing is null now. Core charges: all prices are WITHOUT the core charge, which is refunded when the old transmission goes back. Where shown it was $600 (Reman-Transmission, waived for 30 days), $800 (Nissan), $1,500 (Reman-Transmission 8L90) and $2,000 (GM, earlier trucks); the Honda and Acura pages show no core charge, which does not prove none applies at checkout; a customer whose old unit is not returnable pays it. How solid the labor times are: the low ends for economy, midsize and truck, and the truck high, are manufacturer-stated times for the example vehicle itself (Nissan 7.5 hr, Honda 6.2 hr, GM 5.4-7.4 hr); these are warranty-type times, the low end of what shops bill. The economy and midsize high ends (12 hr) are a consumer guide's general statement, not vehicle-specific. The luxury times are the weakest: the low (6.3 hr) is an Acura time for replacing a torque converter on an RDX, a different model and not a full replacement, and the high (10.9 hr) is the MDX's own bulletin time but also covers replacing the radiator and hoses. So three of the eight hour figures are not for the example vehicle. Confidence is low because the midsize and luxury classes rest on a single dealer-parts retailer each, with no independent remanufacturer's price, and the luxury labor low is not for the example vehicle. An estimate is never a quote and never a diagnosis.
extras: A quote often adds the refundable core charge until the old unit is returned ($600-$2,000 on the listings seen), freight for the unit ($150-$299 on the listings seen), new transmission fluid (Nissan's campaign lists 12 units of CVT fluid and Honda's bulletin 8 quarts), programming or relearning of the transmission control module (two sellers say their unit must be calibrated or reflashed before use), a cooler flush or a new transmission cooler and lines (one remanufacturer requires new coolers; Acura lists 0.9 hr extra where an accessory cooler is fitted), new mounts, seals, exhaust and intake gaskets and one-time-use nuts, coolant, a wheel alignment where the subframe is lowered, a diagnosis fee, shop supplies and sales tax. Four-wheel-drive and all-wheel-drive vehicles take longer (GM lists up to 1.7 hr more for 4WD). A new unit from the dealer, a rebuild of the existing transmission and a used unit are different jobs with different prices and warranties.
